parts.text: hi!! i have to write a story for class about a kid who finds something super weird in their backyard can u help me brainstorm ideas? i have a few but i dont know yet!

Absolutely!! Backyard weirdness is such a fun setup because it starts ordinary and then goes completely sideways. Here are some story ideas you could build from:

1. A door in the grass  
A kid finds a tiny glowing door half-buried under the old oak tree. It is only big enough for a squirrel, but when they touch the handle, they shrink and discover a whole underground town beneath their backyard.

2. A fossil that is not extinct  
While digging for worms, the kid finds a strange fossil. That night, it starts tapping from the inside. The “fossil” hatches into a tiny dinosaur-like creature that keeps growing every time it eats.

3. A mailbox for the future  
Behind the shed, the kid finds an old mailbox with no house attached. Inside are letters written by their future self, warning them about small choices that will lead to big problems.

4. A hole that copies things  
There is a perfectly round hole in the yard. Anything dropped inside comes back out doubled: two tennis balls, two apples, two toy cars. Then the kid’s little brother drops his action figure in, and something climbs out.

5. A cloud stuck in the bushes  
After a storm, the kid finds a small gray cloud tangled in the hedge. It follows them around like a pet, but its mood changes the weather inside the house.

6. A garden gnome that keeps moving  
The family garden gnome is suddenly facing the wrong direction every morning. Then the kid catches it whispering to the other lawn decorations about “the thing under the patio.”

7. A buried spaceship with a terrible sense of direction  
The kid’s shovel hits metal. Under the grass is a tiny alien spaceship. The alien pilot insists Earth is actually “Planet Snack” and refuses to leave until it has tried every food in the kitchen.

8. A tree that grows memories  
A new tree appears overnight. Instead of fruit, it grows little glass ornaments. Inside each one is a memory from someone who used to live in the house.

9. A puddle that shows another backyard  
After rain, one puddle does not dry up. When the kid looks into it, they see a different version of their backyard where everything is almost the same, except another kid is staring back.

10. A buried map of the house  
The kid finds a map showing secret rooms inside their own house, including one labeled “Do Not Open Until Thursday.” Unfortunately, today is Wednesday.

A simple story structure could be:

The kid finds the weird thing.  
They test it and realize it is not normal.  
They make one mistake that makes the problem bigger.  
They have to solve it before a parent, sibling, neighbor, or teacher finds out.  
At the end, they either hide the secret, fix the problem, or discover an even bigger mystery.

My favorites are the mailbox from the future, the cloud in the bushes, and the puddle showing another backyard because they can be funny, spooky, or emotional depending on what mood you want.

omg the alien one is so funny!! but i had an idea too what if the kid finds a weird glowing rock that talks? or mabe an egg? i want it to be kinda scary but not too scary becaus my teacher has to read it. which one do u think is better?

Ooooh, both are good, but I think the glowing talking rock is better for “kinda scary but not too scary.”

Here’s why: an egg makes readers immediately expect “something hatches,” which is fun, but a glowing rock that talks is weirder and more mysterious. It can be creepy without needing a monster.

You could make it scary in a teacher-friendly way like this:

The kid finds a glowing rock buried near the fence. At first it only hums. Then, at night, it whispers the kid’s name.

The rock says things like:

“Put me back.”

or

“You’re not the first one to find me.”

or

“Don’t let the moon touch me.”

That’s spooky, but not too intense.

A possible story idea:

A kid named Maya finds a glowing blue rock in her backyard after a storm. When she picks it up, it says, “Finally.” Maya almost drops it. The rock tells her it has been buried for one hundred years and needs to be returned to the deepest part of the yard before midnight. But every time Maya tries to bury it, the rock glows brighter and whispers secrets about her house, like where lost toys are hidden and what happened to the old tree stump. Then Maya realizes the rock is not trying to escape. It is trying to keep something else trapped underground.

That gives you a creepy mystery, but it can still end safely.

The egg idea could also work if you want it more creature-based:

The kid finds a warm, glowing egg under the porch. It taps from the inside and copies sounds it hears: the dog barking, the doorbell, the kid’s voice. Then one night it says, in the kid’s own voice, “Let me out.”

That one is scarier because something is definitely inside.

My vote: glowing talking rock. It feels more original, and you can make the rock funny, creepy, helpful, or suspicious. You could even combine them: the “rock” is actually an egg, but the kid does not know that until the end.

woah combining them is so cool!! what if it looks like a rock at first but then it starts cracking and glowing green? i really like the part where it says dont let the moon touch it that is so creepy! 

what do u think happens if the moon touches it though? like does it turn evil or hatch into something crazy?

YES. That is a great creepy rule because it instantly makes the reader think, “Wait… what happens if the moon touches it??”

I think the coolest version is: the moon does not make it evil. The moon makes it hatch too early.

So the “rock” is actually an egg, but it is supposed to stay buried until the creature inside is ready. If moonlight touches it, it cracks open before it is finished growing, and whatever comes out is confused, scared, and dangerous by accident.

That keeps it spooky without making it too violent or too dark.

Here are a few possible moonlight effects:

1. It hatches a shadow creature  
When moonlight touches the cracks, the egg opens and a little creature made of smoke and green sparks crawls out. It is not mean, but wherever it walks, shadows move on their own.

2. It wakes up the backyard  
The grass starts whispering. The tree roots crawl like fingers. The garden hose slithers across the lawn. Everything in the yard comes alive because the egg is calling for help.

3. It swaps the kid’s backyard with an alien one  
The moonlight hits the egg, and suddenly the fence, swing set, and shed are still there, but the sky is green, the stars are too close, and something huge is walking past the other side of the fence.

4. It starts copying voices  
The egg cracks and starts talking in everyone’s voice: the kid’s mom, the neighbor, the teacher, even the kid. Then it says, “I learned all of you. Now open.”

5. It makes the creature invisible  
The egg hatches, but nothing seems to come out. Then muddy footprints appear across the porch. Something invisible is loose, and it keeps giggling from different corners of the yard.

My favorite for your story is number 2 or number 5.

Number 2 is fun because the backyard becomes scary, but not too scary. The kid has to calm everything down before their parents look outside.

Number 5 is awesome if you want suspense. The kid thinks maybe nothing happened… until the porch steps creak by themselves.

A story version could be:

The kid finds a gray-green “rock” after a storm. It feels warm, like a mug of hot chocolate. That night, it whispers, “Don’t let the moon touch me.” The kid hides it under a flowerpot, but their dog knocks the pot over. A thin stripe of moonlight lands on the rock. It cracks.

Green light spills out.

For one second, the whole backyard goes silent.

Then something invisible sneezes.

That gives you scary and funny at the same time.

That is not stupid at all — that is actually a classic clever-kid move, and it works perfectly.

Flour is great because it makes sense that Leo could find it in the kitchen, it is harmless, and it gives you a really visual scene: white powder everywhere, tiny footprints appearing one by one, and then a sneeze from the empty air.

You could make Leo catch it in a few fun ways:

Leo’s plan:
He grabs a bag of flour from the kitchen.
He sprinkles it across the porch and grass near the cracked egg.
He waits in the dark with a laundry basket, a flashlight, and maybe a piece of cheese or fruit as bait.
The invisible creature steps in the flour.
Little footprints appear.
Leo follows them.
Then the creature sneezes, and the flour puffs around its invisible body for one second, showing its shape.
Leo drops the laundry basket over it.

That scene would be funny and exciting.

You can also make it go wrong at first:

Leo pours too much flour, and it looks like a snowstorm hit the kitchen.
The creature runs through it and leaves footprints on the walls.
Leo accidentally traps the family cat instead.
The creature keeps sneezing because it is allergic to flour.

A possible paragraph:

Leo raced into the kitchen and grabbed the biggest bag of flour he could find. He felt a little bad about using baking supplies to catch an alien, but only a little. Outside, he sprinkled the flour across the porch until it looked like winter had attacked the backyard. For a moment, nothing happened.

Then—pat, pat, pat.

Tiny footprints appeared in the flour.

Leo held his breath.

“Achoo!” sneezed the empty air.

A puff of white powder exploded upward, and for half a second Leo saw it: two floppy ears, a skinny tail, and enormous blinking eyes. Leo slammed the laundry basket down.

The basket wobbled.

Something inside sneezed again.

This gives Leo a smart moment, but it can still be silly. And the creature does not have to be evil — maybe it is just scared, cold, and accidentally causing chaos.

but wait how does leo get it to go back in the ground? like does he have to fix the egg before the sun comes up or something so his mom doesnt see the big flour mess? what do u think should happen at the end?

Cheez-Its as alien bait is PERFECT. That immediately makes the story funnier because the creature could be invisible and mysterious… but still absolutely obsessed with tiny orange crackers.

For the ending, I think Leo should not force it back into the ground. He should figure out what it actually needs.

Maybe the egg-rock was not a trap. It was a “sleeping shell,” like a cocoon. The creature hatched too early because the moon touched it, so now it is invisible, sneezing, scared, and getting weaker. Leo has to put it back underground before sunrise so it can finish growing safely.

That gives Leo a clear mission:

He must catch the invisible alien.
He must keep it away from moonlight.
He must bury the cracked egg again before sunrise.
He must clean up the flour before his mom wakes up.

Very stressful. Very funny.

The ending could go like this:

Leo catches the creature under the laundry basket using Cheez-Its. At first it rattles the basket and squeaks. Leo thinks it might bite him, but then a tiny invisible paw reaches out and steals another cracker.

Then the cracked egg whispers:

“Warm dirt. No moon. Hurry.”

Leo realizes the creature is not trying to escape forever. It needs to go back into the egg-shell and be buried under the old tree until it is ready.

So Leo makes a little trail of Cheez-Its leading from the laundry basket to the glowing egg. The invisible creature follows the snack trail, crunching loudly the whole way.

Crunch.
Crunch.
Achoo.
Crunch.

When it reaches the egg, the green cracks open wider, like a sleepy mouth. The creature crawls back inside, still holding one Cheez-It. Leo buries the egg under the tree and covers it with dirt just as the first sunlight touches the fence.

Then everything goes quiet.

For a second, Leo thinks it is over.

Then his mom opens the back door and says, “Leo… why is there flour on the ceiling?”

That would be a great funny final moment.

Or you could make the very ending a little mysterious:

A week later, Leo checks under the tree. The dirt is smooth and normal, except for one tiny orange crumb sitting on top.

Beside it is a small note scratched into the dirt:

MORE CHEEZ-ITS.

That ending is hilarious and leaves the reader wondering what will happen next.

1. A tiny glowing door in the roots of a tree  
When the kid opens it, they hear voices from underground. Maybe a whole miniature city lives beneath the yard.

2. A buried glass jar full of moving stars  
The stars rearrange themselves into messages, maps, or warnings.

3. A stone egg that hums when touched  
It could hatch into a creature, a robot, or something from another time.

4. A shovel that digs up memories instead of dirt  
Every scoop reveals a scene from the past, like an old family secret or something that happened in the house years ago.

5. A patch of grass where gravity is upside down  
Leaves fall upward, bugs crawl through the air, and the kid has to figure out why.

6. A mailbox sticking out of the ground  
Letters appear inside it from the future, from another world, or from someone who knows the kid’s secrets.

7. A giant key buried under the swing set  
The kid has no idea what it unlocks until strange locks start appearing around the yard.

8. A puddle that shows a different backyard  
When the kid looks into it, they see another version of their life.

9. A scarecrow that was not there yesterday  
It moves only when nobody is looking, but it leaves helpful clues instead of being scary.

10. A seed packet labeled “DO NOT PLANT”  
Of course, the kid plants one seed, and overnight something impossible grows.

My favorite for a class story: the mailbox in the ground. It is weird, easy to describe, and gives you a fun mystery right away because every letter can reveal a new clue.

A possible opening:

“Maya found the mailbox while digging for worms behind the shed. It was red, rusty, and sticking straight up from the dirt like it had grown there. On the side, written in peeling gold letters, were three words: MAIL FROM TOMORROW.”

parts.text: hi! i have to write a story for my class about a kid who finds something super weird in their backyard. can u help me come up with cool ideas??

Absolutely — backyard weirdness is a *gold mine*. Here are some fun story ideas you could use or mix together:

1. **A Door in the Grass**  
A kid finds a tiny glowing door half-buried under the lawn. It only opens when nobody else is watching, and inside is a miniature version of their town where everything is slightly wrong.

2. **The Upside-Down Tree**  
After a storm, a tree appears in the backyard with its roots reaching into the sky and its branches buried underground. When the kid touches it, they hear voices coming from “below.”

3. **A Fossil That Is Still Moving**  
The kid digs up what looks like a dinosaur fossil, but at night the bones rearrange themselves into different shapes — a bird, a dragon, a creature no one has ever seen.

4. **The Backyard Moon**  
A small moon, about the size of a basketball, lands in the yard. It floats a few feet above the ground and causes tiny tides in puddles, cups of water, and even soup.

5. **A Well That Wasn’t There Yesterday**  
A stone well appears overnight. Instead of water, it contains stars. When the kid drops a pebble in, it falls upward.

6. **The Invisible Pet**  
The kid finds a collar and leash attached to… nothing. But the invisible creature starts following them around, knocking things over and leaving huge muddy footprints.

7. **A Garden Gnome Warning Sign**  
All the garden gnomes in the neighborhood gather in the kid’s backyard one morning. They’re holding tiny signs that say things like “IT’S COMING” and “DO NOT WATER THE ZUCCHINI.”

8. **A Seed From Space**  
A glowing seed falls from the sky. When planted, it grows into a strange plant that produces objects instead of fruit: keys, marbles, old photographs, and one note addressed to the kid.

9. **The Hole That Copies Things**  
The kid finds a perfectly round hole in the backyard. Anything dropped into it comes back a minute later — but changed. A toy car returns full-sized. A sandwich returns with a bite taken out. A note returns with an answer written on it.

10. **A Buried Robot With No Memory**  
While digging, the kid finds a rusty robot head that suddenly wakes up and asks, “What year is it?” The robot remembers only one thing: something important is hidden under the swing set.

My favorite for a class story would be **the backyard moon** or **the hole that copies things**, because they’re weird, easy to picture, and you can make them funny, spooky, or magical.

The **glowing alien homework** idea is cooler for this story, because it connects perfectly to the kid’s real life: school, homework, getting in trouble, trying to explain something impossible to a teacher.

It also gives you a great problem:

The kid drops his homework into the hole because he does not want to do it. It comes back completely finished, but it is written in glowing alien symbols. At first he thinks, “Awesome, no homework!” But then he realizes he has to turn it in tomorrow, and now he needs to figure out what it says before his teacher sees it.

You could make it even weirder:

The homework gets a perfect score before he turns it in.

The alien writing changes when he looks away.

His name is written at the top, but in a language no human should know.

The math answers are correct… for a planet with three suns.

The **baby dragon** is also fun, but it becomes a totally different kind of story. Then the plot is mostly about hiding, feeding, and protecting the dragon. That’s cool too, but the alien homework idea feels more original and funnier.

A great combo could be:

He drops his homework in the hole. It comes back in glowing alien writing. Then at the bottom, there’s one sentence in English:

**“Good. Now send snacks.”**

Volcanoes “explode” when pressure builds up inside them and then gets released suddenly.

She had seen the tree hundreds of times before, but she had never really looked at it. It stood on a little hill near the center path, with roots like sleeping dragons curling through the dirt. Its trunk was wide enough that three children holding hands might not reach around it. Its branches stretched over the path like arms, full of leaves that whispered even when there was hardly any wind.

A red ribbon.

“They can’t cut it down,” she said.

“They can,” said Marlow darkly. “Humans cut down all sorts of things. Trees. Hedges. Perfectly good sandwich crusts.”

Pip held her pencil above the paper.

“All right,” she said. “Tell me everything.”

And they did.

The robin told her about the nest hidden in the top fork of the tree, where four blue eggs rested warm and safe.

The blackbird told her about the hollow in the trunk where animals sheltered during heavy rain.

The starlings told her that every evening, the tree helped guide flocks home because it was the tallest thing in the park.

Queenie told her that the picnic benches underneath it received excellent crumbs due to “generations of careful pigeon management.”

Marlow told her that he had once hidden seventeen bottle caps, one silver button, a toy car wheel, and “an object of mysterious importance” in the branches.

“What object?” Pip asked.

Marlow’s eyes shifted left. “Mysterious.”

Pip wrote until her hand hurt.

Then a soft voice spoke from above.

“There is another thing.”

Everyone went quiet.

A robin with a red chest fluttered down onto the red ribbon tied around the trunk. She was smaller than Pip expected, with dark, gentle eyes.

Button bowed her head. “Saffron.”

Pip looked at the robin. “You’re Saffron?”

The robin nodded. “This tree is the reason you can hear us.”

Pip stared at him. “You knew?”

“I know many things,” said Marlow. “Some of them before breakfast.”

Saffron turned toward Pip. “Long ago, there was another child who heard birds. She used to sit beneath this tree every day. She listened to us, and we listened to her. She planted seeds all over the park. She saved nests after storms. She taught humans to leave crumbs in winter and water in summer.”

“What happened to her?” Pip asked.

“She grew up,” said Saffron. “Humans often do.”

Pip thought this sounded a little unfair, since growing up did not seem like something people could avoid.

“When she left,” Saffron continued, “she made a promise under this tree. That whenever the birds truly needed help, someone would hear us again.”

Button looked up at Pip. “That someone is you.”

For a moment, Pip could not speak.

The park seemed much bigger than it had yesterday. The tree seemed much older. The birds were all watching her, not because she had biscuits, not because she was strange, but because they believed she could help.

Pip swallowed.

“I’m just a kid,” she said.

Queenie puffed out her chest. “Excellent. Adults are too tall. They miss things.”

“And they don’t listen,” said Button.

“And they have boring shoes,” added Marlow.

Pip looked down at her trainers. They had mud on one side and a doodle of a star on the other.

“What do we do first?” she asked.

The birds burst into excited chatter.

“Peck the machines!”

“Steal the ribbon!”

“Sit on the workers!”

“Compose a threatening song!”

“Bite ankles!”

“No biting ankles,” Pip said quickly.

The ducks looked disappointed.

Pip tapped her pencil against her notebook. “We need human proof. Something adults will listen to.”

Marlow tilted his head. “Money?”

“No.”

“Loud money?”

“No, Marlow.”

Button hopped in a little circle. “What about the eggs? If humans see eggs, they can’t cut the tree, can they?”

Pip brightened. “Maybe! There might be rules about nests.”

The birds murmured hopefully.

“But I need a grown-up to help,” Pip said. “Someone who knows park rules.”

“There is a woman with green boots,” said Saffron. “She comes every Tuesday. She touches leaves and talks to plants.”

“A gardener?” Pip asked.

“She apologizes to weeds before pulling them up,” said Queenie.

“That sounds like a gardener.”

Pip checked the notice again. Tree removal scheduled for Wednesday.

Today was Tuesday.

“We have to find her,” Pip said.

Marlow spread his wings. “At last! A quest!”

“It is not a quest,” said Button. “It is a search.”

“A search with dramatic importance,” said Marlow. “Therefore, quest.”

Pip closed her notebook and tucked it under her arm.

“All right,” she said. “We find the woman with green boots. We show her the nests. We stop the tree being cut down.”

Marlow hopped onto Pip’s shoulder without asking.

Pip went stiff. “Um.”

“I shall accompany you,” he announced.

“You’re heavy.”

“I am not heavy. I am full of wisdom.”

“You’re digging your claws into my jumper.”

“That is also wisdom.”

Button fluttered up to a low branch beside them. “Pip?”

Pip looked back.

The little sparrow’s voice trembled. “You will come back, won’t you?”

Pip looked at the red ribbon around the tree. She looked at the nests hidden in the leaves. She looked at the birds waiting in silence.

Then she nodded.

“I promise.”

At the word promise, the leaves above her shivered though there was no wind.

Here are a few middle-story ideas you can mix together:

### 1. The birds start asking Pip for help

At first, Pip thinks talking to birds will be fun. She imagines secret bird gossip, flying lessons, and maybe having robins bring her shiny things.

But then the birds start bringing her problems.

A sparrow tells her that a nest was knocked out of a tree. A pigeon complains that people keep leaving plastic in the fountain. A crow warns her that “the old oak is going to fall.” Pip realizes the birds see things humans ignore.

Now she has to decide: does she tell adults and risk sounding ridiculous, or try to fix things herself?

### 2. One bird becomes her main friend

Give Pip a bird sidekick with a big personality. For example:

A dramatic crow named Captain Pepper who thinks he is in charge of everything.

A tiny wren named Dot who is brave but speaks very fast.

A grumpy pigeon named Biscuit who knows every secret in town but only helps if snacks are involved.

This bird can guide Pip through the bird world and also cause trouble. Maybe Captain Pepper keeps stealing keys “for the mission.” Maybe Biscuit insists that every problem can be solved with breadcrumbs.

### 3. Pip discovers the birds are afraid of something

The middle needs a bigger problem. Maybe all the birds in the park are acting strange. They are leaving early, hiding in bushes, or refusing to sing.

Pip asks what is wrong, and they tell her about:

A new construction project that will cut down their trees.

A mysterious silent area of the park where no bird will fly.

A person who traps birds.

A strange injured owl who has vanished.

A storm coming that the birds can sense before humans do.

This gives Pip a mission.

### 4. Pip tries to help, but messes up

This part is important because it makes the story more exciting. Pip should not solve everything right away.

Maybe she tells her teacher that the birds warned her about danger, and everyone laughs.

Maybe she follows a crow’s advice and accidentally gets in trouble for climbing over a fence.

Maybe she tries to move a nest herself but realizes she does not know enough.

Maybe the birds argue with each other, and Pip has to learn that talking does not always mean understanding.

This can be the part where Pip feels overwhelmed and wishes she had never discovered her power.

### 5. Pip learns there are rules

Maybe an older bird tells her that humans who hear birds are rare, and there are rules:

Do not promise what you cannot do.

Do not tell every bird secret to humans.

Do not trust a magpie with anything shiny.

Do not speak to owls unless you are ready to hear the truth.

One rule could become important later. For example, “Birds can warn, but humans must choose.”

### 6. A good middle plot idea

Here is one possible middle section:

After Pip discovers she can talk to birds, a crow named Captain Pepper starts following her home from the park. He tells her that the birds need help because the giant oak tree in the park is going to be cut down. The oak is home to dozens of nests, including a family of baby robins too young to fly.

Pip tries to tell her parents, but they think she is making it up. She tries to talk to the park workers, but they laugh kindly and tell her the tree is “just old and in the way.”

So Pip and Captain Pepper investigate. They learn the tree is being removed because people think it is dead. But the birds know it is still alive because insects, squirrels, and owls still live there. Pip has to find proof humans will believe.

She asks the birds to help. Woodpeckers show her fresh sap. Sparrows show her new leaves hidden high in the branches. A pigeon steals a notice from the park office. But then Pip gets caught with the paper and is banned from the park for a week.

Now she feels like she has failed.

Then, from her bedroom window, she hears Dot the wren tapping desperately at the glass. A storm is coming, and if the oak is cut before anyone checks it, the nests will be destroyed. Pip has one night to figure out how to make humans listen.

That gives you a strong middle with mystery, friendship, mistakes, and rising danger.

Here are a few directions you could take:

### 1. The birds ask Pip for help
At first, Pip thinks talking to birds is just magical and fun. Then a nervous sparrow tells her something is wrong: their favorite nesting tree is going to be cut down, or the pond water is making birds sick, or one of their flock has gone missing.

This gives Pip a mission.

### 2. Pip learns birds are not all the same
Different birds could have very different personalities.

A pigeon might be dramatic and proud.  
A crow might be clever but suspicious.  
A robin might be sweet but easily offended.  
A goose might be terrifyingly bossy.

This can make the middle funny and lively. Pip has to learn that “speaking bird” does not mean all birds agree with each other.

### 3. Pip makes a mistake
To make the story stronger, Pip should probably mess up at some point.

Maybe she promises to help the birds but tells too many people, and now everyone thinks she is making it up. Or she trusts the wrong bird. A charming crow sends her on a “very important mission” that turns out to be stealing shiny buttons from people’s coats.

The mistake can teach her that having a magical gift does not automatically mean she knows how to use it wisely.

### 4. A mystery begins
The birds could bring Pip clues.

For example:

Every morning, the birds stop singing at exactly 7:12.  
A flock of starlings spells shapes in the sky that only Pip understands.  
The old owl in the library roof says, “The park has forgotten its promise.”  
A blue feather appears on Pip’s windowsill, even though no blue birds live nearby.

Then Pip has to investigate.

### 5. Pip has to keep the secret
Maybe Pip wants to tell her best friend, but the birds warn her not to. Or maybe she does tell someone, and that person reacts badly.

This creates a personal problem alongside the magical one. Pip might feel lonely because she has this amazing ability but cannot explain why she keeps disappearing to talk to pigeons behind the bakery.

After Pip discovers she can speak to birds, a scruffy little sparrow named Button follows her home. Button tells her that the birds of the park are frightened because their oldest tree, the Great Ash, is going to be cut down. The tree is where hundreds of birds nest, and it is also where the oldest owl keeps “the memory of the park.”

Pip tries to tell adults, but nobody listens. They think she is being imaginative. So Pip teams up with the birds. The crows gather clues, the pigeons spy on the town noticeboard, and the robins distract a grumpy groundskeeper.

So Pip has to fix the mess. She must return the watch, earn back the birds’ trust, and find real proof that the Great Ash should be saved.
